# Akittijātaka (Ja 480)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Akittijātaka* (Ja 480) is a birth story of the Bodhisatta recounting his life as the wealthy brāhmaṇa Akitti of Benares, identified with the sage Agastya and also addressed by the family name Kassapa [Speyer 1895; Mein Da 2015]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related this story while residing at Jetavana in connection with a generous donor living in Sāvatthī [Fausböll 1887]. Seeking renunciation, Akitti distributed his immense riches, departed Benares through what became remembered as the Akitti Gate (*Akittidvāra*) and Akitti Ferry (*Akittitittha*), and entered the ascetic life accompanied initially by his sister [Fausböll 1887; Mein Da 2015]. He later developed meditative insight in a garden at Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam before retreating to supreme solitude on Ahidīpa (subsequently known as Karadīpa, near Nāgadīpa off northern Sri Lanka), subsisting solely on kara-leaves sprinkled with water [Adikaram 1946; Monius 2001; Mein Da 2015].

Akitti's austere tapas heated the heavenly throne of Sakka, who visited him in the guise of a brāhmaṇa mendicant to test his detachment [Sahni 2008; Mein Da 2015]. Akitti joyfully offered his meagre food to the visitor for three consecutive days without keeping any for himself [Sahni 2008]. When an impressed Sakka offered him boons, the ascetic rejected all worldly desires, requesting instead spiritual blessings such as never being subjected to the sight, sound, or company of a fool, and remaining free from anger, greed, and insatiability [Anandajoti 2010; Speyer 1895]. Akitti's sacrifice is celebrated across canonical and post-canonical literature—such as the *Cariyāpiṭaka* and *Jātakanidānakathā*—as a prime embodiment of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) [Appleton 2010; Gaffney 2003].

 Machine text-reuse alignments by DharmaNexus corroborate these connections, identifying shared material between Ja 480 and Ja 547 (§16.4–17.4) as well as Pv 21 (§16.3–18.1), along with extensive parallels in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā*, and *Kaṇhajātaka* (Ja 440) [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, the narrative corresponds to the tale of Agastya in Āryaśūra’s Sanskrit *Jātakamālā* and exhibits textual alignment with the Tibetan *Udānavargavivaraṇa* [DharmaNexus; Speyer 1895].
